newsitem.title: USA: Sources close to Fed say odds favor May rate hike.
newsitem.headline: Sources close to Fed say odds favor May rate hike.

text.p: The Federal Reserve is likely to raise short-term interest rates by a quarter percentage point next week in another bid to insure against potential overheating of the economy, sources close to the Fed said.
"There is a very good chance the Fed will do another 25 basis points (quarter percentage point), and virtually no chance it will do 50 basis points," one source told Reuters.
A second source close to the central bank noted that U.S. financial markets were not yet helping the Fed restrain growth, indicating the need for another move.
The central bank's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee raised the federal funds rate that banks charge each other for short-term loans by a quarter point to 5.50 percent in March.

It was the first time in more than two years that the Fed raised rates to address the potentially inflationary strength of the economy. Fed policy-makers meet next Tuesday to consider whether to raise rates.
The Fed left the discount rate, the rate it charges banks for direct loans, unchanged in March.
The first source said that whether a hike in the fed funds rate would be accompanied by a discount rate increase "would be entirely at the discretion of the (Fed) chairman" Alan Greenspan.

"If you don't believe a fundamental change has taken place in the economy, you have to be wary about the numbers that came out," the source said, referring to the 5.6 percent rise in the Gross Domestic Product in the first quarter.
The source also was referring to April's 4.9 percent unemployment rate that pointed to very tight labour markets.
Analysts have cited higher-than-expected growth in the labour force as a reason why tight labour markets have not yet translated into rapidly rising wages.
"That last report scored a point to the view the period of rapid labour force growth is over," the source added, noting the decline in the size of the workforce from March to April.
The source acknowledging, however, that the Fed was expecting a slowdown "from the clearly unsustainable" pace of the past two quarters.

"The question is when the slowdown will come. The answer keeps being postponed," the source pointed out. "The slowdown was supposed to come in the fourth quarter and Q4 came as a surprise on the upside. At this point, some of us are getting wary about confidently predicting the slowdown is imminent."
Private economists are forecasting a second-quarter slowdown as the large surge in inventories in the first quarter should subtract from subsequent growth.
The second source said the Fed's move in March had failed to spark any market restraint and that more tightening was necessary.
"The only thing that would make the Fed pause is if we get a lot more slowdown here. It's the third and fourth quarter that are at issue here," the source stressed.
